title: Phase Space Reorganization and Travelling Wave Emergence Driven by Non-Kerr Effects in Nonparaxial Optical Media
authors: Naresh Saha, Nirmoy Kumar Das, Ashoke Das, Arnob Ray
abstract: In this article, the nonlinear Helmholtz equation with non-Kerr nonlinearity, such as self steepening and self frequency shift, is considered. A travelling wave transformation is applied, and the extended nonlinear Helmholtz equation is reduced to a Hamiltonian dynamical system. Then, the reduced Hamiltonian system is analyzed by classification of equilibrium points, phase space analysis, and the construction of exact wave solutions. The relationship between the reduced dynamical coefficients and the original physical parameters is further established through a parameter space analysis. It is shown that self steepening directly modifies the reduced dynamics, whereas self frequency shift acts through the compatibility condition for the real travelling wave reduction. Together, these non-Kerr effects reshape the phase space geometry and travelling wave structure. Localized and periodic travelling waves are obtained, with their existence determined by the balance among dispersion, nonparaxiality, Kerr nonlinearity, and non-Kerr effects. Furthermore, a periodically forced version of the reduced system is examined to study the transition from regular to irregular dynamics. It has been observed that external forcing can induce complex oscillatory behavior. Bifurcation analysis, time series evolution, phase space analysis, largest Lyapunov exponent, and Poincaré section demonstrate the emergence of quasiperiodic and chaotic responses under sufficiently strong forcing. All analytical branches are verified through full-equation residual evaluation, while a few selected branches are additionally examined through direct numerical propagation and robustness tests under complex Gaussian perturbations. The results show that self steepening directly renormalizes the effective nonlinear dynamics, whereas self frequency shift restricts the admissible real-envelope travelling wave manifold.
summary: This paper analyzes pulse propagation in nonparaxial optical media by reducing the governing equation to a Hamiltonian system. It demonstrates that incorporating non-Kerr nonlinearities (Self Steepening and Self Frequency Shift) fundamentally alters the phase space structure of the traveling waves. Furthermore, it characterizes the transition from regular to chaotic wave dynamics when the system is subjected to external periodic forcing.
main_problem: The study investigates how non-Kerr nonlinear effects, specifically self steepening (SS) and self frequency shift (SFS), fundamentally reorganize the phase space geometry and traveling wave structure in nonparaxial optical media.
main_result: These non-Kerr effects reshape the underlying Hamiltonian dynamics; SS directly renormalizes the effective nonlinearity, while SFS constrains the admissible real travelling wave manifold. The system can also exhibit complex quasiperiodic or chaotic responses under external forcing.
method: The analysis involves reducing the nonlinear Helmholtz equation via a traveling wave ansatz to a planar Hamiltonian dynamical system. This is followed by phase space analysis, bifurcation theory for forced systems, and chaos diagnostics like Lyapunov exponents.
model_or_system: The model is based on the Nonlinear Helmholtz Equation (NLH) describing pulse propagation in nonparaxial optical media. The dynamics are reduced to a conservative Hamiltonian $H(V, Q)$ governing the envelope amplitude $V$ and its derivative $Q$.
key_observables: Localized/periodic wave existence, phase space geometry (separatrices, equilibria), Largest Lyapunov Exponent ($\Lambda_{\max}$), and Poincaré section structure.
important_parameters: The effective nonlinear coefficients $\alpha$ and $ eta$, which depend on physical parameters like dispersion, nonparaxiality, Kerr nonlinearity, SS, and SFS terms.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on applying a symmetry-guided traveling wave ansatz to reduce the NLH equation to a planar Hamiltonian system. The study also examines periodically forced extensions of this reduced system.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate parameter space diagrams showing how varying physical coefficients determine the signs of the effective nonlinear coefficients $\alpha$ and $ eta$, which govern the phase plane topology.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the reduction to a Hamiltonian system using traveling wave transformations. It then analyzes the resulting planar dynamics via equilibrium point classification and phase space analysis, detailing how SS and SFS modify the conserved Hamiltonian structure. Finally, it extends this analysis to periodically forced systems, employing Lyapunov exponents and Poincaré sections to map out transitions to chaos.
why_interesting: This work applies advanced dynamical systems tools (Hamiltonian mechanics, bifurcation theory) to model complex wave phenomena in nonlinear optics, providing a rigorous mathematical framework for understanding how higher-order physical effects alter stable wave solutions.

Figure 2: Representative phase portraits of the reduced planar system Eq. (6) for four sign combinations of (α, β). Each trajectory lies on an invariant Hamiltonian level set H(V, Q) = h. Saddles (red open circle) generate separatrices and organize global transitions between orbit classes, whereas centers (red filled circle) are surrounded by closed invariant curves corresponding to bounded oscillatory wave states. The representative reduced parameters are (a) α = 5.45, β = 0.4; (b) α = 0.64, β = −0.64; (c) α = −0.952, β = 3.17; (d) α = −0.55, β = −1.2.

Figure 3: Bifurcation diagrams and largest Lyapunov exponent of the forced reduced system. Peak values Qmax (blue) and largest Lyapunov exponent Λmax (red) are plotted as a function of forcing amplitude λ for two representative unforced regimes, Case 2 (α = 0.64, β = −0.64, panels (a, b) and Case 4 (α = −0.55, β = −1.2, panels (c, d), with forcing frequency Γ = 2π. Panels (a, c) use the initial condition (V0, Q0) = (0.005, 0.005), while panels (b, d) use (V0, Q0) = (1.0, 1.0). The transition between regular quasiperiodic motion and irregular chaotic dynamics is identified in the bifurcation structure and confirmed by the largest Lyapunov exponent.
